title: No. 1 overall seed UCLA eliminated in baseball regionals after Saint Mary's walks it off in extras
article_text:
No. 1 overall seed UCLA eliminated in baseball regionals after Saint Mary's walks it off in extras
For the second straight year, the No. 1 overall seed has crashed out of the NCAA baseball regionals. UCLA’s season came to a close after a 6-5 loss to Saint Mary’s in extra innings.
The Gaels picked up the one-run win after sending the game to extras with a game-tying run in the bottom of the ninth. Then, Saint Mary’s stunned the Bruins in the 10th inning with Makoa Sniffen’s walk-off base hit that sent Cody Kashimoto home for the win. Both of those high-stakes RBIs came with two outs on the board.
It’s the second time in three days that UCLA has been upset by Saint Mary’s. The Gaels shocked the Bruins in the regionals’ opener on Friday. Jacob Johnson gave his team the lead with a solo homer in the top of the ninth, and Cam Staton closed it out on the mound to give Saint Mary’s a 3-2 win.
Prior to 2025, no No. 1 seed had ever failed to at least make the regional final, per ESPN. Now, UCLA joins Vanderbilt, which fell to Wright State last year, as the second straight No. 1 seed to stumble early.
Saint Mary’s will now face Cal Poly for a chance to stay alive, in a rematch of the Gaels’ 14-1 loss to the Mustangs on Saturday. Because this stage of the tournament is double elimination, Saint Mary’s will have to beat Cal Poly twice (once on Sunday and once on Monday) in order to advance.
UCLA, meanwhile, will be heading home. The Bruins’ early exit also marks another poor showing from the Big Ten, baseball-wise, leaving Oregon and USC as the only teams left in the conference — for now.

rationale.Attribution & Causation: The article implies that UCLA's loss is a significant event, using phrases like 'crashed out' and 'stunned the Bruins', which may indicate a biased attribution of causality.
rationale.Availability & Salience: The article highlights the unusual nature of UCLA's loss, mentioning that it's the second straight year a No. 1 seed has been eliminated, which may be an example of availability heuristic.
rationale.Framing & Anchoring: The article frames the loss as a significant upset, using phrases like 'shocked the Bruins' and 'stunned the Bruins', which may influence the reader's perception of the event.
rationale.In-Group & Social: The article mentions the Big Ten conference's poor showing, which may indicate a bias towards in-group favoritism or a negative perception of out-groups.

judgments.rationale: The excerpt 'UCLA’s season came to a close after a 6-5 loss to Saint Mary’s in extra innings' does not necessarily imply that UCLA's loss is due to their own failure, as it is a neutral statement of fact. The second excerpt 'The Bruins’ early exit also marks another poor showing from the Big Ten, baseball-wise' could be seen as attributing the performance to the team, but it is more related to the team's overall performance rather than a specific failure.

The excerpts 'For the second straight year, the No. 1 overall seed has crashed out of the NCAA baseball regionals' and 'Prior to 2025, no No. 1 seed had ever failed to at least make the regional final, per ESPN' both use recent, vivid cases to imply a broader trend, which is a classic example of the Availability Heuristic bias.

The excerpts 'For the second straight year, the No. 1 overall seed has crashed out of the NCAA baseball regionals', 'UCLA’s season came to a close after a 6-5 loss to Saint Mary’s in extra innings', 'The Gaels stunned the Bruins in the 10th inning with Makoa Sniffen’s walk-off base hit that sent Cody Kashimoto home for the win', and 'Prior to 2025, no No. 1 seed had ever failed to at least make the regional final, per ESPN' all use language that frames the events in a specific, often negative, light, which is a clear example of the Framing Effect bias.

The excerpts 'For the second straight year, the No. 1 overall seed has crashed out of the NCAA baseball regionals' and 'Prior to 2025, no No. 1 seed had ever failed to at least make the regional final, per ESPN' do provide reference points, but they are more related to establishing a pattern or providing context rather than anchoring the reader to a specific value or idea.

The excerpts 'UCLA, meanwhile, will be heading home. The Bruins’ early exit also marks another poor showing from the Big Ten, baseball-wise' and 'Both of those high-stakes RBIs came with two outs on the board' do not provide sufficient evidence to suggest that the author is exhibiting an in-group bias, as the language used is more neutral and descriptive rather than emotive or biased.

The excerpt 'Prior to 2025, no No. 1 seed had ever failed to at least make the regional final, per ESPN. Now, UCLA joins Vanderbilt, which fell to Wright State last year, as the second straight No. 1 seed to stumble early' does present a negative outcome, but it is a factual report of an event rather than an emphasis on the negative aspect, and the overall tone of the article is more neutral than negative.
